one_liner: Rust message-streaming server whose v0.7.0 rewrite on thread-per-core io_uring (compio) cuts tail latency versus its Tokio/epoll build.
what_it_does: Apache Iggy is a persistent append-only log (streams, topics, partitions, consumer groups) in the same role as Kafka, served over TCP, QUIC, WebSocket and HTTP. From v0.7.0 the server runs one pinned shard thread per core, each with its own io_uring instance through the compio runtime, in place of Tokio's work-stealing executor. The entry is this server rewrite, not a reusable event-loop library: you get it by running the iggy-server binary or the apache/iggy Docker image, and clients keep using the Iggy SDKs.
how_it_is_fast: Completion-based io_uring replaces readiness-based epoll for sockets and, more importantly, replaces Tokio's blocking thread pool (up to 512 threads) for file writes and fsync. Each shard is a pinned thread that owns a set of partitions assigned by hash, so the data plane has no work stealing and no cross-thread locks; when a client writes to an explicit partition on the wrong shard, its TCP socket fd is handed to the owning shard. Stream and topic metadata has a single writer (shard 0) that publishes to the other shards through a left-right structure fed by flume channels (the 'shared something' design); the rings are created with IORING_SETUP_COOP_TASKRUN and no helper thread pool.
when_to_use: You run Iggy on Linux (kernel 5.19+) and care about P99.9/P99.99 write latency more than peak throughput.
Many partitions and producers per node: the published gap grows from roughly even at 8 producers to 57-60% lower P95-P99 at 32 producers x 32 streams, with P50 also down from 2.21 to 0.77 ms there.
Durable writes with fsync on every batch where throughput and P95+ matter: the fsync runs show about 18% more throughput and about 45% lower P95 than the Tokio build.
Dedicated hosts where one pinned shard per core is acceptable and the kernel and seccomp policy allow io_uring.
You are on Iggy 0.5.x or earlier (Tokio) and want a lower write tail without changing client code.
when_not_to_use: Small deployments of about 8 partitions or producers: P95 and P99 were 8% and 3% worse than the Tokio build there; only P99.9 and above improved.

Median-sensitive fsync-per-batch writes: the dashboard reports show P50 rising from 1.53 to 3.54 ms (16 partitions) and from 2.66 to 6.25 ms (32 partitions) on v0.7.0, although mean and P95+ fell; the blog tables start at P95.
You need more peak throughput: the non-fsync comparisons were capped at 1 GB/s by the benchmark's rate limit, so no throughput gain is shown outside the fsync runs.
Skewed traffic with a few hot partitions: shards do not steal work, and the blog lists hot-shard balancing (e.g. splitting a partition across shards) as unsolved future work.
Native Windows (the v0.7.0 server has compile_error!("iggy-server doesn't support windows."); use WSL or Docker), containers with Docker's default seccomp profile, or kernels older than 5.19.

integration.form: built binary (iggy-server, Docker image apache/iggy); not a library
integration.dependencies: compio 0.18 with the io-uring driver (at tag server-0.7.0), left-right, flume, DashMap, mimalloc (default global allocator), hwlocality/hwloc for NUMA-aware core allocation
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.93.0 pinned by rust-toolchain.toml at tag server-0.7.0 (edition 2024; current master pins 1.98.0 with rust-version 1.95); Linux kernel 5.19+ per the Docker docs
integration.platforms: Linux for io_uring; macOS builds use compio's non-io_uring driver and have had shard startup panics on some targets (Intel/Rosetta); native Windows unsupported at v0.7.0; CPU architecture requirements not documented
integration.thread_safety: Server process: one pinned shard thread per core (sharding cpu_allocation, default numa:auto); each partition is owned by one shard; stream/topic metadata has a single writer (shard 0) with left-right readers on the other shards
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial - a server upgrade from Iggy 0.5.x (Tokio) to 0.7.0, not a swappable event loop; the host kernel and container runtime must allow io_uring

gotchas: Docker needs --security-opt seccomp=unconfined (or a custom profile allowing io_uring_setup, io_uring_enter and io_uring_register) and --ulimit memlock=-1:-1; the README also lists --cap-add=SYS_NICE. The server prints these hints when ring creation fails with EPERM or ENOMEM.

Idle servers can show IO pressure (PSI) and iowait near 100% because shards parked in io_uring_enter are counted as iowait on kernels 6.5+. Issue #3507 (open) calls it cosmetic, but it breaks iowait-based alerting.

Socket migration only applies to explicit partition ids: Balanced and MessagesKey partitioning skip the fd handoff and are routed to the owning shard instead. The benchmark used pinned producers, which is the migration-friendly case.

io_uring alone did not produce the tail gain: the intermediate v0.6.1 shared-nothing build on the dashboard had P99.99 of 208 ms at 32x32 (v0.5.0: 27.5 ms). The drop came with v0.7.0's shared-metadata redesign.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Iggy when you want a finished message-log server that already applies the Seastar-style thread-per-core design in Rust; monoio or ringline are the runtimes to build your own io_uring server on, and Seastar is the C++ framework Iggy's design follows.
verified_claims_summary: The maintainers compared Iggy v0.5.0 (Tokio: epoll for sockets, a blocking thread pool for files) with v0.7.0 (compio io_uring, thread-per-core) using iggy-bench pinned-producer over TCP (1000-byte messages, 250 per batch, 1 GB/s rate limit) on AWS i3en.3xlarge (Xeon Platinum 8259CL, 12 vCPU, Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.17), with client and server on separate hosts. At 32x32, P99 fell from 4.52 to 1.82 ms, at 16x16 P99.99 fell from 86.3 to 7.17 ms, and fsync runs gained 18% throughput; the percentiles are averages of per-producer percentiles, each version ran on a different EC2 server/client pair on the same day, the toolchain and flags are not stated, and the two versions differ in far more than the I/O backend.
status_note: Active Apache Software Foundation project (Apache-2.0) with daily commits; server 0.9.0 (September 2026) has since added VSR clustering on the same shard design, so v0.7.0 is no longer the latest release.
